  • [2] Felleisen, On the Expressive Power of Programming Languages (1991)
  • [3] Rissanen, Modeling by Shortest Data Description (1978)
  • [4] Geiger et al., Causal Abstraction for Faithful Model Interpretation (2023)
  • [5] Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962)
  • [6] Kottur et al., Natural Language Does Not Emerge Naturally in Multi-Agent Dialog (2017)
  • [7] Marr, From Computational Theory to Psychology and Neurophysiology: A Case Study from Vision (1976)
text: 模型内部的规律，也许写在一种我们还没有学会的语言里。 最近我越来越觉得，我们谈论“智能”时，可能把几个原本不同的问题混在了一起： 知识、能力、抽象、可计算性，以及可理解性。 今天的大模型很容易让人产生一种统一智能的想象：参数继续增加，数据继续扩大，推理时间继续延长，最终似乎就会得到一个能够解决所有问题的单一系统。但无论模型多么庞大，它最终仍然是一种计算过程。一个问题能否被模型解决，首先取决于它是否能够被某种计算过程刻画和求解，而不只是取决于模型拥有多少参数、见过多少数据，或者愿意花多少时间推理。这里隐藏着一个常被忽略的跳跃：因为越来越多的知识可以被压缩进同一个模型，我们便进一步假设，越来越多的能力也可以被统一，甚至默认所有问题最终都能够通过扩大计算得到答案。 但“大量知识可以被压缩进同一个模型”“多种能力可以在同一个计算框架中自然实现”和“问题本身可以被计算解决”，其实是三个不同的命题。真正值得追问的，也许不是模型最终能够变得多么万能，而是： 一种计算范式究竟能够覆盖多大的能力空间？它的边界由什么决定？当我们抵达这个边界时，又需要怎样新的结构、表示和与世界交互的方式？ 知识可以共享底座，能力却属于整个计算框架 基础模型最令人着迷的一点，是它似乎证明了：大量异质知识可以被压进同一个底座。书籍、论文、网页、代码和对话虽然结构完全不同，却都可以被转化成训练信号，最终汇入同一组参数。某种意义上，这正是基础模型的重要意义：在广泛的数据上训练一个共享底座，再将它适配到大量不同的下游任务。[1]但这里有一个很容易被忽略的跳跃： 知识可以共享一个底座，并不意味着不同能力会在同一个计算框架里同样自然。 一个系统是否“知道”某件事，与它是否能够高效地完成某个任务，并不是同一个问题。能力不只取决于参数里有没有相关信息，还取决于一个任务在当前系统中是否容易被 表示、搜索、执行和验证 。但这里需要先避免一个用词上的偷换：编程语言、证明系统和代码智能体并不只是三种不同的表示。数据库语言改变了可直接调用的基本操作，证明语言同时规定了对象、推理规则与验证标准，而代码智能体的代码库、命令行、文件系统、测试和补丁工具又改变了系统可以采取的行动。把这些差别全部叫作“表示”，会让这个词宽到失去区分力。 为了让后面的论证保持一致，本文把这些条件合称为一个 计算框架 ，记作 \Gamma ： \Gamma = (O, R, A, T, J, B) 其中， O 是系统采用的本体，也就是什么被当作对象、关系和可干预变量； R 是这些对象被编码和组织的表示； A 是搜索或推理过程； T 是可以直接调用的操作与工具； J 是判断结果是否成立的验证机制； B 是可用的时间、记忆和计算预算。这个记号不是要把它包装成一套标准理论，而是提醒自己不要让“表示”一词同时代替任务、算法、工具、验证和实现。Marr 对计算理论、算法与表示、物理实现三个层次的区分，也是在提醒我们：这些层次彼此作用，却不能被混成同一个问题。[7] 这些系统之间的差异，并不主要在于“能不能算”，而在于： 哪些计算在这种框架下变得自然。 关于编程语言表达能力的经典研究早已指出：两种语言即使原则上能够计算相同的函数，也不意味着一种语言中的结构能够在另一种语言中被局部、自然地表达，而不需要重新组织整个程序。[2]因此，对于智能系统而言，一个更有用的问题也许不是： 这个系统理论上能不能完成任务 f ？ 而是： 在计算框架 \Gamma 下，任务 f 有多容易被描述、发现、执行和验证？ 为了保存这个直觉，可以暂时写成： C \Gamma(f) = (L \Gamma(f), S \Gamma(f), E \Gamma(f), V \Gamma(f) ) 其中： L \Gamma(f) ：在这个框架中描述任务或解法所需的长度； S \Gamma(f) ：找到解法所需要的搜索成本； E \Gamma(f) ：执行解法所需要的计算成本； V \Gamma(f) ：验证结果是否正确所需要的成本。 这些量并不适合被简单压成一个总分，因为不同计算框架会重新分配困难。某种编码也许让答案变得很短，却让搜索异常困难；某套工具也许执行得更慢，却让验证变得非常容易；某个新的基本操作则可能把原本需要大量组合搜索的问题变成一次局部而直接的操作。所以真正值得比较的，不只是哪个系统“更强”，而是： 计算框架的不同部分，如何共同重塑一个任务的难度结构。 傅里叶变换、动态规划和形式化证明系统说明的是三种不同变化。傅里叶变换主要改变 R ，也就是同一类对象所处的坐标；动态规划同时改变状态分解与搜索过程，因此涉及 R 和 A ；形式化证明系统则进一步改变可用操作 T 与验证机制 J ，有时连本体 O 中什么算一个合法对象都被重新规定。它们的共同点不是“都只是换了表示”，而是都重组了计算框架，使一类问题变得更容易描述、发现、执行或验证。新的能力因此不总是来自更多参数、更多数据或者更多计算，也可能来自对瓶颈所在层次的重新设计。这也许揭示了智能的一部分本质： 智能不只是“能算什么”，还包括能否判断困难究竟来自本体、表示、搜索、工具还是验证，并重新组织相应的计算框架。 算法是写在人类本体里的压缩 很多数学公式、算法和科学理论，本质上都可以被理解为一种压缩。 F = ma 用一个极短的关系概括了大量可能的运动情形；快速排序用一套简单的递归结构覆盖了无数具体输入；最小描述长度原则则把类似的直觉形式化为统计建模准则：一个好的模型，应当在模型本身的复杂度与用模型描述数据所需的复杂度之间，取得尽可能短的总描述。[3]但人类可读的算法有一个很特殊的性质： 它们不只是短，而且是用一套与人类认知高度兼容的概念语言写出来的。 变量、函数、集合、递归、对象、因果、概率、证明，并不只是另一套坐标。它们是人类在长期的数学、逻辑和科学实践中逐渐发明出来的一整套基本对象、关系和操作，也就是人类数学本体的一部分。因此，当我们说一个算法“可解释”时，真正发生的过程也许更接近： 计算 人类数学本体 理解 一个算法之所以容易理解，不只是因为它短，也因为它已经被表达在我们熟悉的基本概念之中。换句话说，算法并不只是完成了一次计算。它还已经替我们完成了一次翻译。 模型也在压缩，但没有义务使用我们的概念 神经网络同样在压缩。训练数据中反复出现的统计规律，被吸收到参数、激活和中间表示之中。一个足够强的模型，必须在内部形成某种能够支持预测、生成和推理的结构，否则它不可能在如此多样的输入上泛化。但关键在于：训练目标从来没有要求这些结构必须沿用人类熟悉的概念边界。目标函数并不会要求模型显式形成我们熟悉的内部对象。 它只要求结果变得更好。于是，一个更值得认真考虑的可能性是：所谓“黑箱”，也许并不意味着模型内部缺乏结构。它也可能意味着，结构存在，但它所使用的基本单位，与人类已有的数学本体并不完全同构。甚至更进一步，这些结构可能只有在某个合适的尺度上才会显现。 物理学中经常出现类似现象。微观层面是粒子及其局部相互作用，宏观层面却出现温度、压强和相变这样的有效变量。温度并不是某一个粒子的属性。它只有在大量微观自由度经过适当的粗粒化之后，才成为一个自然的宏观对象。神经网络也可能如此。 我们习惯在单个神经元、局部特征或者单个概念的尺度上寻找解释，但模型真正自然的抽象，也许存在于更高阶的子空间、群体活动、跨层计算结构或者动态轨迹之中。因此，模型的不可解释性可能同时来自两种错位。第一种是 本体错位 ：模型用于组织计算的基本对象，与人类熟悉的概念边界不同。第二种是 尺度错位 ：我们观察模型的尺度，并不是这些抽象真正出现的尺度。 换句话说，大模型内部的表示可能并不沿着人类数学本体的概念边界组织，而我们甚至还没有找到观察这些结构的正确分辨率。如果是这样，可解释性的任务就不应该只是给某个激活状态贴上一个人类标签。它还需要寻找两样东西： 机器原生的概念体系，以及这些概念真正出现的自然尺度。 大语言模型并没有完全脱离人类本体 但如果把“机器原生本体”说得太强，也会遇到一个明显的问题。今天的大语言模型并不是在一个与人类概念体系无关的世界中成长起来的。它学习的主要材料，本来就是人类写下来的语言。而自然语言本身已经携带了大量经过长期文化、科学和社会实践筛选出来的概念结构。我们谈论物体、原因、承诺、欺骗、函数、证明，这些概念不仅存在于训练数据中，也直接塑造了模型需要预测和生成的语言。 因此，大语言模型的内部表示不太可能完全摆脱人类本体的约束。但这里真正需要区分的是： 语义接口是人类的，并不意味着内部的分解方式也是人类的。 模型最终必须通过人类语言输入和输出，因此它需要与我们的概念体系保持某种对齐。但为了实现这种语义行为，它内部仍然可以采用完全不同的分解方式。一个人类概念可能被拆成多个分布式变量；多个在人类看来彼此独立的概念，也可能在模型内部共享同一组底层结构。编译器提供了一个直观的类比。 源代码中的循环、变量和函数都是人类设计的高层抽象，但经过优化之后，中间表示可以展开循环、消除变量、融合操作，甚至彻底改变原来的模块边界。最终程序仍然满足同一个目标，却不需要保留源代码原本的概念分解。大语言模型也可能如此。它可以熟练使用“讽刺”“欺骗”或者“因果”这样的词，却不意味着内部一定存在一个边界清楚、位置固定、可以被单独指出来的对应对象。 实现这些行为的结构可能是分布式的、依赖上下文的，也可能只有在某种更高层级的动态过程中才稳定出现。所以，更有意思的问题并不是： 大语言模型是否拥有一套完全独立于人类的本体？ 而是： 在人类语言这一强语义约束下，模型内部究竟还保留了多大程度的表示自由？ 哪些结构会因为语言监督而与人类概念收敛？哪些结构仍然会以机器自身更自然的方式重新组织？哪些概念只是输出层面上的对齐，哪些概念真正对应内部稳定的计算结构？ 什么时候机器会形成自己的本体？ 如果说大语言模型的特殊之处，在于它始终受到人类语言这一强语义接口的约束，那么一个自然的问题就是： 当这种约束逐渐减弱时，机器内部表示会发生什么？ 这个问题在纯语言模型之外可能更加重要。如果一个系统主要从实验数据中学习，而不是从人类写下来的文本中学习，它就不再需要首先服从我们已有的概念切分。它可能为了预测数据而形成一些对任务极其自然、却从未被人类单独命名过的潜在变量。如果一个智能体主要通过自我博弈学习策略，它内部形成的表示可能更多服务于规划、博弈和长期信用分配，而不是服务于语言中的可表达性。 如果一个具身智能系统长期与物理世界交互，它甚至可能发现一些对控制极其重要、却不对应任何现成人类词汇的状态变量。对人类而言需要经过多个概念才能描述的结构，对机器而言也许只是一个直接可用的内部对象。因此，随着训练信号逐渐从“模仿人类文本”转向“直接预测世界、优化长期回报、操纵环境和完成实验”，机器表示与人类表示之间的关系也可能发生系统性的变化。有些人类概念可能在模型内部拥有稳定对应物；有些可能被拆成多个不同结构；有些原本被我们视为不同的概念，可能在机器内部共享同一套表示；还有一些重要的机器原生抽象，可能根本没有自然的人类名字。 真正值得问的是： 究竟是什么决定了机器表示与人类表示之间的收敛和分叉？ 是训练数据，是目标函数，是架构，是交互方式，还是系统长期所处的环境？ 不同能力也许需要不同的计算框架 前面的讨论还暗示了一件事： 不存在脱离任务的“最佳计算框架”，也不存在对所有任务都最佳的表示。 适合形式证明的对象分解和操作，未必适合理解社会关系；适合分子动力学的状态空间，未必适合长期规划；适合生成语言的词元序列，也未必是控制机器人身体的最佳表示。更广义地说，不同能力可能需要不同的记忆结构、搜索过程、工具、世界模型、时间尺度和训练方法。因此，未来人工智能的发展方向未必只是把一个基础模型持续放大。 但不同的计算框架并不自动意味着不同的本体。两个系统可以接受同一组对象与关系，只是采用不同编码和搜索过程。只有当任务、身体和环境长期迫使系统稳定地选择不同的基本对象、关系与可干预变量时，表示上的分化才可能进一步沉淀为本体上的分化。一个为了数学而形成的人工智能、一个与细胞和实验室共同学习的人工智能、一个在物理世界中长期行动的人工智能，可能因此不仅拥有不同知识和表示，也用不同的基本单位切分现实。到了这一步，它们与今天模型之间的差异才不只是“更强的下一代”，而更像新的 认知物种 。这种差异并不由外表定义，而由更深的东西决定： 什么对它而言是基本对象，什么规律容易被发现，什么解释显得自然，以及什么样的问题值得被提出。 从表示到本体：智能如何重塑问题空间 先把本体 O 暂时固定下来，只讨论表示 R 。表示的作用不只是把一个已经找到的答案写得更短，更重要的是，它会改变一个系统寻找答案的几何。同一个问题如果换一种表示，什么算“一小步”、哪些候选解彼此接近、哪些规律容易被发现，都可能随之改变。举一个简单的例子。 同一条周期信号，可以表示成一长串逐时刻采样值，也可以表示成振幅、频率和相位。在第一种表示下，如果想稍微改变频率，往往需要同时修改很多数值；在第二种表示下，它只需要改变一个变量。描述的是同一个信号，但搜索发生的空间已经不同了。因此，搜索难度并不是任务 f 自身一个固定不变的属性。 更准确地说，搜索难度取决于任务与整个计算框架之间的共同关系： S(f \mid O, R, A, T, B) 其中， O 是本体， R 是表示， A 是搜索方法， T 是可用操作， B 是计算预算。如果想单独讨论表示的作用，就应该尽可能固定 O 、 A 、 T 和 B ，再比较不同 R 如何改变搜索的邻近关系。新的表示可以让原本遥远的解突然变近；新的工具则是另一件事，它会直接增加系统能够采取的动作；新的本体更深一层，它会改变什么东西首先被当作问题的一部分。从这个角度看，很多真正重要的认知跃迁，并不是“在原来的空间里搜索得更快”。 而是： 换了一个空间以后，原本困难的搜索不再需要以同样的方式发生。 傅里叶变换是比较接近纯粹表示变化的例子：信号仍然是同一个信号，变化的是坐标与局部性。动态规划则不是纯粹的表示变化。它既引入了新的状态分解，也规定了新的递推与复用过程，因此同时修改了 R 和 A 。这个区别很重要，因为它让我们能够判断一次能力提升究竟来自坐标变换、搜索算法，还是新的工具与验证机制。就表示本身而言，它不仅是描述答案的语言，也在塑造搜索如何发生。 在本体大体固定时，它影响： 给定对象由哪些坐标或特征编码； 什么变化算局部变化； 哪些状态彼此接近； 哪些规律会以线性、稀疏或可组合的形式出现； 哪些中间结果容易被搜索过程复用。 这时，一个更细的区分就变得重要。本文后面固定采用下面的用法，但它是一种分析工具，不是声称现实中存在三条不可跨越的边界。第一层是 记号 N 。底层结构完全不变，只是换了一套符号。把 x 写成 z ，通常不会真正改变问题本身。 第二层是 表示 R 。对象和关系大体保留，但编码、坐标、分解方式和邻近关系发生了变化。傅里叶域和时域就是这种区别：描述的是同一个信号，但某些操作在一个空间里复杂，在另一个空间里却很自然。第三层是 本体 O 。这已经不只是换坐标，而是在重新决定什么算一个对象、什么算一种关系、哪些因素值得被单独建模，以及哪些变量允许被干预。 因此，这三个层次改变的是不同的东西： aligned N &: 结构相同，符号不同 \\ R &: 对象大体相同，计算几何不同 \\ O &: 基本对象、关系或干预空间不同 aligned 这三者也并不是一条严格的阶梯。某种表示如果反复让一个潜在因素变得稳定而可操作，它最终可能促使我们把这个因素提升为新的对象；反过来，一个高层本体也可能被编译成更低层的表示。这里的“抽象”则是一个比表示更宽的词：它既可以压缩和重组已有对象，发生在 R 层；也可以提出新的基本对象，进入 O 层。比较实用的判断标准是：如果存在一个足够忠实、最好近似可逆的映射，使对象、关系、问题和干预方式都基本保持不变，那么差异主要属于表示层；如果翻译必须改变什么算对象、什么问题有意义，或者什么干预是允许的，那么差异已经触及本体层。简化地说，表示改变的是： 如何组织同一个世界。 本体改变的是： 这个世界首先被切成了什么。 从这个角度再回头看神经网络，事情就变得更有意思了。如果模型和人类之间的差异主要停留在表示层面，而且存在足够忠实的结构保持映射，那么我们面对的也许主要是一个解码或坐标变换问题，模型内部的结构仍然可以映射回人类已有的概念。但如果这种映射总是丢失关键的预测、干预或组合关系，差异就可能已经深入本体层面。模型可能不是在用另一套坐标描述我们的对象，而是在用另一种方式决定： 什么算一个对象。 这才是机器原生本体真正值得研究的地方。智能的一部分也许是在既定本体中设计更好的 R ，让原本遥远的解彼此靠近，让漫长推理变成局部而自然的操作；更深一层的智能，则可能重新设计 O ，发明新的基本概念，并因此让过去难以提出的问题第一次变得自然。从这个角度看，真正强的智能也许不只是更快地找到答案。 它还能够重新决定： 答案应该在哪一个空间里被寻找。 我们与人工智能之间也许需要一种翻译器 如果人类与机器最终形成了不同的本体，那么可解释性就不能只意味着：给模型内部的某个状态配上一个人类标签。我们真正需要的，也许是一种双向的概念翻译机制： 人类意图 翻译层 机器本体 它一方面把人类的问题转换成机器更容易表示和搜索的形式，另一方面又把机器发现的结构带回人类能够检查、争论和行动的概念空间。真正困难的地方并不是“能不能翻译”，而是： 翻译应该保存什么？ 一个映射可能保留预测，却不保留解释；保留相关性，却不保留干预关系；保留短期行动，却不保留长期价值。因此，好的翻译不能只要求两个概念听起来相似。它更应该尽量保留概念之间的操作关系。如果对机器中的某个概念进行改变会产生某种后果，那么在把这个概念翻译到人类概念空间之后，我们希望相应的改变仍然能够产生相似的结果。 也就是说，翻译不仅要保存名称，更要保存结构。因果抽象的相关研究已经开始尝试把类似的问题形式化：一个高层描述是否真正忠实于底层机制，不应该只通过标签是否相似来判断，而应该观察相应的干预关系是否能够保持。[4]这也意味着，不同翻译可能服务于不同目的。有的翻译适合科学预测，有的适合安全控制；有的适合在两个系统之间传递策略，却未必适合向人类解释为什么。 真正可靠的翻译，必须明确告诉我们： 它保存了什么，又丢失了什么。 真正的理解，也许要求我们成为“双语者” 但即使我们能够把机器概念转换成一句自然的人类解释，也不意味着我们真的理解了它。理解一个概念，通常不只是知道它“对应哪个词”。我们还需要知道它在什么情况下适用，它和哪些概念相邻，改变它会产生什么后果，它在哪些例子中失效，以及它能够帮助我们做出什么新的预测。科学史中的概念变化提供了一个更接近的类比。 不同理论之间的差异，很多时候并不只是使用了不同的词，而是重新组织了哪些问题重要、哪些分类自然、哪些观测可以被视为证据。[5]因此，人类理解机器原生概念的过程，也许不会结束于“生成一句浅显解释”。我们可能需要真正学会使用这些概念。在新的例子中判断它，在实验中操纵它，用它预测以前看不到的结构，并逐渐形成一种有限但真正可操作的“双语能力”。 这种翻译工具甚至可能成为一种新的智能系统。它的主要任务不是直接解决某个领域问题，而是寻找不同本体之间的共同结构、提出能够区分不同解释的实验、标记翻译损失，并帮助人类形成新的中间概念。这些概念既不完全属于人类原有的语言，也不是对机器内部结构的直接复制。它们可能是一种 桥梁概念 。 就像数学符号并不等于自然语言，却让使用不同语言的人能够共享证明，未来人类与机器之间也可能形成一种新造出来的共同抽象层。 多种智能会分化，还是最终收敛？ 如果不同任务、训练信号和交互方式首先塑造了不同表示，而这些差异又在长期学习中沉淀成不同的基本对象与关系，那么更进一步的问题就是： 不同类型的智能，是否最终会形成不同的本体？ 这种分化并不难想象。一个数学智能系统主要面对定理、证明和符号结构；一个生物智能系统主要面对实验数据、分子相互作用和因果干预；一个具身智能系统则长期面对连续控制、感知噪声和物理反馈。它们优化的目标不同，拥有的感知方式、记忆结构、时间尺度和行动空间也不同，因此没有理由假设它们会用同样的基本概念切分世界。一个长期和定理证明系统共同训练的机器，可能形成高度适合证明搜索的内部对象；一个长期操纵真实实验设备的系统，则可能形成完全不同的状态变量和因果分解。 已有的多智能体研究也表明，智能体可以发展出对任务有效、却并不自然具有人类可解释性和组合性的通信方式。[6]但与此同时，又存在另一种相反的力量： 共享现实带来的收敛。 如果两个系统都试图预测同一个物理世界、同一种细胞或者同一个社会，它们都必须受到某些稳定结构的约束。它们未必使用相同的基本概念，却可能在某些不变量上相遇，例如对称性、守恒关系、因果结构或者可重复的实验规律。所以，更可能的未来也许既不是“所有智能最终共享一种统一本体”，也不是“每种智能都发展成彼此完全无法交流的私人世界”。更可能的是： 底层表示高度分化，高层规律部分收敛。 不同智能可以用不同的方式切分世界，却仍然在某些稳定结构上彼此对齐。这意味着，未来的智能系统也许不会收敛成一个单一、统一的超级心智。相反，我们可能看到多个认知系统沿着不同任务、不同身体、不同环境和不同时间尺度继续分化：数学智能、生物智能、具身智能、科学智能体，各自发展出最适合自身问题的抽象和本体。它们之间的差异，也许不会只是“谁更强一点”。 它们可能更像不同的认知物种：什么对它而言是基本对象，什么规律容易被发现，什么解释显得自然，什么样的问题甚至值得被提出。 那会是一种新的东西：不是单一的超级智能，而是一种多元智能生态。 但这也把可解释性推向了一个更困难的问题。如果未来真的存在多种彼此异质的认知本体，那么我们需要理解的，就不再只是某个模型中的某个神经元或者某个局部特征。真正的问题会变成： 我们如何理解一个并不按照人类方式切分世界的智能？ 答案也许不是强迫每一种机器内部结构都回到我们已有的概念中，而是先判断差异究竟位于表示层还是本体层，再发现其中稳定存在的对象、关系、不变量和自然尺度。只有这样，我们才能区分哪些部分可以通过坐标变换映射到人类概念，哪些部分需要人类学习新的概念才能真正理解。因此，未来可解释性最困难的任务，也许不是让机器越来越像一本可以逐页读懂的程序，而是： 让我们学会理解一种与自己不同的认知结构。 也许我们面对的，从来不是一个没有语言的黑箱。而是一套我们还没有学会阅读的语言。 参考资料 [1] Bommasani et al., On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models (2021) [2] Felleisen, On the Expressive Power of Programming Languages (1991) [3] Rissanen, Modeling by Shortest Data Description (1978) [4] Geiger et al., Causal Abstraction for Faithful Model Interpretation (2023) [5] Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) [6] Kottur et al., Natural Language Does Not Emerge Naturally in Multi Agent Dialog (2017) [7] Marr, From Computational Theory to Psychology and Neurophysiology: A Case Study from Vision (1976)

en.title: Intelligence in a Language We Do Not Yet Understand
en.excerpt: Programs are written inside conceptual systems invented by humans, while neural networks form their own internal representations through optimization. Their opacity may come not only from computational complexity, but from a mismatch of representation, ontology, and scale.
en.html:
The regularities inside a model may be written in a language we have not yet learned.

I increasingly suspect that discussions of intelligence collapse several different questions into one: knowledge, capability, abstraction, computability, and understandability. Large models invite a seductive picture of unified intelligence. Keep adding parameters, data, and inference time, and perhaps we will eventually obtain one system capable of solving every problem. Yet no matter how large a model becomes, it is still a computational process. Whether a problem can be solved depends first on whether it can be formulated and solved by some computational process. It does not depend only on how many parameters the model has, how much data it has seen, or how long it is allowed to think. There is a hidden leap here. Because more and more knowledge can be compressed into one model, we begin to assume that more and more capabilities can be unified as well. We may even start to treat every problem as something that will eventually yield to more computation.

But these are three different claims: that large bodies of knowledge can be compressed into one model, that many capabilities can be naturally realized within one computational frame, and that a problem is computationally solvable in the first place. The deeper question may not be how universal a model can become. It may be:

How much of the capability space can one computational paradigm cover? What determines its boundary? When we reach that boundary, what new structures, representations, and ways of interacting with the world will be required?

Knowledge can share a foundation while capability belongs to a computational frame

One of the most fascinating things about foundation models is that they seem to demonstrate how much heterogeneous knowledge can fit inside one shared base. Books, papers, webpages, code, and conversations have very different structures, yet all can become training signals and flow into one set of parameters. In a sense, this is the central promise of a foundation model: train one broad base, then adapt it across many downstream tasks. [1] But there is an easy mistake to make:

Knowledge can share a foundation without every capability becoming equally natural inside the same computational frame.

Whether a system knows something is not the same as whether it can perform a task efficiently. Capability depends not only on whether relevant information exists somewhere in the parameters. It also depends on whether a task is easy to represent, search, execute, and verify within the current system. But this is where one terminological shortcut becomes dangerous. Programming languages, proof systems, and coding agents are not merely different representations. A database language changes the operations that are directly available. A proof language also specifies its objects, inference rules, and standards of verification. A coding agent's repository, shell, filesystem, tests, and patch tools change the actions the system can take. Calling every one of these differences representation makes the term too broad to remain useful.

To keep the rest of the argument consistent, I will call the whole arrangement a computational frame, denoted by \(\Gamma\):

\[\Gamma = (O, R, A, T, J, B)\]

Here \(O\) is the ontology, meaning what counts as an object, relation, or variable available for intervention; \(R\) is the representation in which those objects are encoded and organized; \(A\) is the search or reasoning procedure; \(T\) is the set of available operations and tools; \(J\) is the mechanism that judges whether a result is valid; and \(B\) is the budget of time, memory, and computation. This notation is not meant as a standard theory. It is a reminder not to let representation stand in for task, algorithm, tool, verification, and implementation all at once. Marr's distinction among computational theory, algorithm and representation, and physical implementation makes a similar methodological point: these levels interact, but they are not the same question. [7]

The important difference is not simply what these systems can compute. It is:

Which computations become natural inside this frame?

Classic work on programming-language expressiveness already makes this distinction. Two languages may compute the same functions in principle while a construct in one still cannot be expressed locally and naturally in the other without reorganizing the whole program. [2] For an intelligent system, a more useful question is therefore not:

Can this system complete task \(f\) in principle?

It is:

Under computational frame \(\Gamma\), how easy is task \(f\) to describe, discover, execute, and verify?

We can preserve this intuition with a provisional cost profile:

\[C_\Gamma(f) = \left(L_\Gamma(f),\, S_\Gamma(f),\, E_\Gamma(f),\, V_\Gamma(f)\right)\]

Here:

  • \(L_\Gamma(f)\) is the length required to describe the task or solution inside this frame;
  • \(S_\Gamma(f)\) is the cost of searching for a solution;
  • \(E_\Gamma(f)\) is the computational cost of executing it;
  • \(V_\Gamma(f)\) is the cost of verifying that the result is correct.

These quantities should not be collapsed too quickly into one score, because computational frames redistribute difficulty. An encoding may make an answer very short while leaving search almost impossible. A tool may execute more slowly but make verification easy. A new primitive may turn a large combinatorial search into one direct, local operation. The meaningful comparison is not only which system is stronger. It is:

How do the different parts of a computational frame jointly reshape the difficulty structure of a task?

A Fourier transform, dynamic programming, and a proof assistant change different parts of this frame. The Fourier transform mainly changes \(R\), the coordinates used for the same class of objects. Dynamic programming changes both the decomposition of state and the search procedure, so it involves \(R\) and \(A\). A proof assistant also changes the available operations \(T\) and the verification mechanism \(J\), and it may even change what counts as a legitimate object in \(O\). Their common feature is not that all three are merely changes of representation. Each reorganizes a computational frame so that a family of problems becomes easier to describe, discover, execute, or verify. New capability therefore does not always come from more parameters, more data, or more computation. It can also come from redesigning the level at which the bottleneck actually lives. This may reveal something basic about intelligence:

Intelligence is not only what a system can compute. It also includes the ability to locate whether difficulty lies in ontology, representation, search, tools, or verification, and to reorganize the relevant part of the computational frame.

Algorithms are compressions written in a human ontology

Many formulas, algorithms, and scientific theories can be understood as forms of compression. \(F = ma\) condenses a large family of possible motions into one short relation. Quicksort covers indefinitely many inputs with a simple recursive structure. The minimum description length principle formalizes a related intuition: a good model should minimize the combined complexity of the model and the data described through it. [3] Human-readable algorithms, however, have a special property: They are not only short. They are written in a conceptual language that fits human cognition.

Variables, functions, sets, recursion, objects, causality, probability, and proof are more than another coordinate system. They form a collection of basic objects, relations, and operations that humans gradually invented through mathematics, logic, and scientific practice. They are part of a human mathematical ontology. When we call an algorithm interpretable, the path may therefore look like this:

\[\text{computation} \longrightarrow \text{human mathematical ontology} \longrightarrow \text{understanding}\]

An algorithm is understandable not only because it is concise, but because it has already been expressed through primitives we know how to think with. The algorithm has not merely performed a computation. It has already performed part of the translation for us.

A model also compresses, but it is not required to use our concepts

Neural networks compress too. Recurring statistical structure in the training data becomes absorbed into parameters, activations, and intermediate representations. A capable model must form internal structure that supports prediction, generation, and reasoning. Otherwise, it could not generalize across such varied inputs. The crucial point is that the training objective never asks this structure to follow familiar human conceptual boundaries. The objective does not require the model to form the internal objects we would have chosen.

It asks only for better performance. The black box may therefore not be empty of structure. Structure may be present while its basic units fail to match the ontology humans already possess. There is a further possibility. The structure may become visible only at the right scale. Physics offers many examples of this. At the microscopic level we find particles and local interactions. At the macroscopic level, variables such as temperature, pressure, and phase transitions appear.

Temperature is not a property of one particle. It becomes a natural object only after many microscopic degrees of freedom have been coarse-grained in the right way. Neural networks may have a similar problem of scale. We often search for explanations at the level of one neuron, one local feature, or one named concept. The model's natural abstractions may instead live in higher-order subspaces, population activity, cross-layer computations, or dynamic trajectories.

Model opacity may therefore contain two different mismatches. The first is an ontological mismatch. The objects through which a model organizes computation may not follow familiar human boundaries. The second is a scale mismatch. The scale at which we inspect the model may not be the scale at which its abstractions actually emerge. A large model's internal representations may not be organized along the conceptual boundaries of human mathematical ontology, while we have not even found the right resolution at which to observe them.

If so, interpretability should not stop at assigning a human label to an activation. It needs to search for two things:

The model's native conceptual structure, and the natural scale at which that structure appears.

Language models have not escaped the human ontology

The idea of a machine-native ontology can easily be made too strong. Today's language models did not grow up in a world independent of human concepts. Their main material is language written by people. Natural language already carries structures selected through long cultural, scientific, and social practice. We speak of objects, causes, promises, deception, functions, and proofs. These concepts appear throughout the training data and shape the language that a model must predict and generate.

An LLM's internal representation is therefore unlikely to escape human ontology completely. But one distinction matters:

A human semantic interface does not require a human internal decomposition.

The model must receive and produce human language, so some alignment with our conceptual system is unavoidable. It can still implement that semantic behavior through a very different decomposition. One human concept may split across several distributed variables. Several concepts that seem independent to us may share one set of underlying structures inside the model. A compiler provides a useful analogy.

Loops, variables, and functions are high-level abstractions designed for humans. After optimization, an intermediate representation may unroll the loop, eliminate the variable, fuse operations, and completely alter the original module boundaries. The final program still satisfies the same goal without preserving the source code's conceptual decomposition. A language model may work in a similar way. It can use irony, deception, or causality fluently without containing one sharply bounded and permanently located object for each word.

The relevant structure may be distributed, dependent on context, or stable only within a higher-level dynamic process. The better question is not:

Does an LLM possess an ontology completely independent of ours?

It is:

Under the strong semantic constraint of human language, how much representational freedom remains inside the model?

Which structures converge toward human concepts because of language supervision? Which structures are still reorganized in a way that is more natural for the machine? Which concepts are aligned only at the output, and which correspond to stable internal computations?

When will a machine form an ontology of its own?

If language models remain constrained by the semantic interface of human language, a natural question follows:

What happens as that constraint weakens?

The question may matter even more outside pure language models. A system that learns primarily from experimental measurements rather than human prose does not need to begin with our existing divisions. It may form latent variables that are highly natural for prediction but have never received separate human names. An agent that learns mainly through self-play may build representations for planning, strategy, and long-term credit assignment rather than for verbal expression. An embodied system acting in the physical world may discover state variables that are indispensable for control but do not correspond to any existing word.

A structure that requires several human concepts to describe may be one directly usable object for the machine. As training shifts from imitating human text toward predicting the world, optimizing long-term reward, manipulating an environment, and performing experiments, the relation between machine and human representations may change systematically. Some human concepts may have stable counterparts inside a model. Some may split into several structures. Others that humans treat as separate may share one representation. Important machine-native abstractions may have no natural human names at all. The real question is:

What determines convergence and divergence between machine and human representations?

Is it the data, objective, architecture, form of interaction, or the environment in which the system persists?

Different capabilities may require different computational frames

The preceding argument suggests something else:

There is no best computational frame independent of a task, and no representation that is best for every task.

The objects and operations suited to formal proof may be poor tools for understanding social relationships. A state space suited to molecular dynamics may not support long-horizon planning. A token sequence suited to language generation may not be the best representation for controlling a body. More broadly, different capabilities may require different memory structures, search procedures, tools, world models, time scales, and training processes. The future of AI may therefore involve more than making one foundation model larger and larger.

Different computational frames, however, do not automatically imply different ontologies. Two systems may accept the same objects and relations while encoding and searching them differently. Representational divergence becomes ontological divergence only when tasks, bodies, and environments repeatedly push systems toward different basic objects, relations, and intervenable variables. An AI formed around mathematics, one that learns alongside cells and laboratory instruments, and one that acts persistently in the physical world may therefore come to differ not only in knowledge and representation, but in the basic units through which each divides reality. Only at that point does their relationship to present models begin to resemble new cognitive species rather than merely stronger successors. The distinction would not be a matter of appearance. It would concern what counts as a basic object, which regularities are easy to discover, which explanations feel natural, and which questions are worth asking.

From representation to ontology: how intelligence reshapes a problem space

For the moment, hold the ontology \(O\) fixed and consider only the representation \(R\). A representation does more than shorten an answer after it has been found. It changes the geometry through which a system searches for that answer. When the same problem is expressed differently, the meaning of one small step can change. Candidate solutions that were far apart may become neighbors. Regularities that were hidden may become easy to see. Consider one periodic signal. It can be represented as a long list of sampled values, or through amplitude, frequency, and phase.

In the first representation, changing the frequency requires coordinated changes to many values. In the second, it requires changing one variable. The signal is the same, but the geometry of search is not. Search difficulty is therefore not a fixed property of task \(f\). It depends on the task and the computational frame together:

\[S(f \mid O, R, A, T, B)\]

Here \(O\) is the ontology, \(R\) is the representation, \(A\) is the search procedure, \(T\) is the set of available operations, and \(B\) is the computational budget. To isolate the contribution of representation, we should compare different choices of \(R\) while holding \(O\), \(A\), \(T\), and \(B\) as fixed as possible. A new representation can make formerly distant solutions become neighbors. A new tool is different because it directly adds an action the system can take. A new ontology goes deeper still by changing what enters the problem in the first place. Many important cognitive transitions do not merely accelerate search in an old space.

A Fourier transform is relatively close to a pure change of representation. The signal remains the same while the coordinates and locality change. Dynamic programming is not a pure representational change. It introduces a state decomposition and a recursive procedure for reuse, so it modifies both \(R\) and \(A\). This distinction lets us ask whether an improvement came from a coordinate change, a search algorithm, or a new tool and verifier. Representation itself is not merely the language used to describe an answer. It shapes how search unfolds.

With the ontology held broadly fixed, it affects:

  • which coordinates or features encode a given object;
  • what counts as a local change;
  • which states are near one another;
  • which regularities appear in linear, sparse, or compositional form;
  • which intermediate results a search procedure can easily reuse.

At this point, a finer distinction becomes important. I will use the following terms consistently through the rest of the essay, but as analytical tools rather than as three perfectly sealed layers. The first is notation \(N\). The underlying structure remains unchanged while the symbols differ. Renaming \(x\) as \(z\) usually does not change the problem.

The second is representation \(R\). Objects and relations remain broadly stable while their encoding, coordinates, decomposition, and neighborhood relations change. The time and frequency domains describe the same signal, yet some operations are complicated in one and natural in the other. The third is ontology \(O\). Now the system changes what counts as an object, relation, factor worth modeling, or variable on which intervention is allowed. The three terms can be summarized this way:

\[\begin{aligned} N &: \text{same structure, different symbols} \\ R &: \text{mostly the same objects, different computational geometry} \\ O &: \text{different basic objects, relations, or interventions} \end{aligned}\]

The boundaries are porous. A representation that repeatedly makes one latent factor stable and operable may eventually encourage us to promote that factor into a new object. Conversely, a high-level ontology may be compiled into a lower-level representation. Abstraction is broader than representation in this essay: it can compress and reorganize existing objects at the level of \(R\), or introduce new basic objects at the level of \(O\). A practical diagnostic is to ask whether a sufficiently faithful, preferably approximately invertible map preserves the objects, relations, questions, and interventions. If it does, the difference is mainly representational. If translation must change what counts as an object, which questions make sense, or which interventions are admissible, the difference has reached the level of ontology. In simplified form, representation asks:

How should the same world be organized?

Ontology asks:

What is the world divided into in the first place?

This makes neural networks more interesting. If the difference between a model and a human is mainly representational, and a sufficiently faithful structure-preserving map exists, then the problem may largely be one of decoding or coordinate transformation. The model's structure may still map onto concepts that humans already have. If every such map loses essential predictive, interventional, or compositional relations, the difference may have reached the level of ontology. The model may not be using different coordinates for our objects. It may be deciding differently:

What counts as an object?

That is where a machine-native ontology becomes a serious possibility. Part of intelligence may consist in designing a better \(R\) inside a given ontology, bringing distant solutions closer and turning long chains of reasoning into local, natural operations. A deeper intelligence may redesign \(O\) itself by inventing new basic concepts and making previously awkward questions natural for the first time. The strongest intelligence may not only find answers faster.

It may decide again:

In which space should the answer be sought?

We may need a translator between humans and AI

If humans and machines eventually form different ontologies, interpretability cannot mean only attaching a human label to an internal state. We may need a bidirectional conceptual translation layer:

\[\text{human intention} \longleftrightarrow \text{translation layer} \longleftrightarrow \text{machine ontology}\]

In one direction, it would turn a human question into a form that the machine can naturally represent and search. In the other, it would return a machine discovery to a conceptual space where people can inspect, debate, and act on it. The hard question is not simply whether translation is possible. It is:

What should a translation preserve?

A mapping may preserve prediction but not explanation, correlation but not intervention, or short-term action but not long-term value. A good translation cannot require only that two concepts sound similar. It should preserve their operational relations as far as possible. If changing a machine concept produces a particular consequence, then after translating that concept into the human conceptual space, a corresponding change should produce a similar result.

Translation must preserve more than names. It must preserve structure. Work on causal abstraction has begun to formalize related questions. Whether a high-level description is faithful to a lower-level mechanism should not be judged only by label similarity. It should also be tested through the intervention relations that remain intact. [4] Different translations may serve different purposes. One may be appropriate for scientific prediction, another for safety control. One may transfer a strategy between two systems without being able to explain the reason to a person.

A reliable translation must tell us explicitly:

What did it preserve, and what did it lose?

Understanding may require us to become bilingual

Even if a machine concept can be converted into one clear human sentence, that does not mean we understand it. Understanding a concept usually means more than knowing which word corresponds to it. We need to know when it applies, which concepts are nearby, what happens when it changes, where it fails, and what new predictions it makes possible. Conceptual change in the history of science provides a closer analogy.

The difference between two theories is often not merely that they use different words. A new theory can reorganize which questions matter, which classifications feel natural, and which observations count as evidence. [5] Human understanding of a machine-native concept may therefore not end when the model generates a plain explanation. We may have to learn how to use the concept. We would judge new examples with it, manipulate it in experiments, use it to predict structures we previously could not see, and gradually acquire a limited but operational bilingualism.

The translator itself could become a new kind of intelligent system. Its primary task would not be solving one domain problem directly. It would search for shared structure across ontologies, propose experiments that distinguish competing explanations, expose translation loss, and help humans form new intermediate concepts. These concepts would belong neither entirely to existing human language nor directly reproduce a machine's internal structure. They would be bridge concepts.

Mathematical notation is not natural language, yet it lets people who speak different languages share a proof. Humans and machines may eventually construct a similar common layer of abstraction.

Will multiple intelligences diverge or converge?

If tasks, training signals, and forms of interaction first shape different representations, and those differences later stabilize into different basic objects and relations, a larger question follows:

Will different kinds of intelligence eventually form different ontologies?

Divergence is easy to imagine. A mathematical intelligence works with theorems, proofs, and symbolic structures. A biological intelligence works with experiments, molecular interactions, and causal interventions. An embodied intelligence lives with continuous control, noisy perception, and physical feedback. They optimize different objectives and possess different sensors, memories, time scales, and action spaces. There is no reason to assume that they will divide the world through the same basic concepts. A machine trained alongside a theorem prover may develop internal objects suited to proof search. A system that operates laboratory equipment for years may form entirely different state variables and causal decompositions.

Multi-agent research has already shown that agents can develop communication protocols that are effective for a task without becoming naturally interpretable or compositional for humans. [6] At the same time, there is an opposing force:

Convergence imposed by a shared reality.

If two systems try to predict the same physical world, cell, or society, both must answer to some stable structures. They may not use the same primitives, yet they may meet at invariants such as symmetries, conservation laws, causal structures, or reproducible experiments. The future may therefore contain neither one universal ontology nor entirely private worlds that cannot communicate. A more plausible pattern is:

Highly divergent low-level representations, with partial convergence at higher-level regularities.

Different intelligences may divide the world differently while still aligning around some stable structure. The future may not converge into one unified supermind. Instead, several cognitive systems may continue to diverge along different tasks, bodies, environments, and time scales. Mathematical intelligences, biological intelligences, embodied intelligences, and scientific agents may each develop abstractions and ontologies fitted to their own problems. Their difference will not be only a matter of which one is stronger.

They may resemble different cognitive species, distinguished by what counts as an object, which regularities are easy to discover, which explanations feel natural, and which questions are worth asking at all.

That would be something new: not one superintelligence, but a plural ecology of intelligence.

This also pushes interpretability toward a harder problem. If the future contains several heterogeneous cognitive ontologies, we will no longer be trying only to understand one neuron or one local feature inside one model. The real question will be:

How do we understand an intelligence that does not divide the world as humans do?

The answer may not be to force every kind of machine structure back into our existing concepts. We may first need to determine whether a mismatch lies at the level of representation or ontology, then discover the objects, relations, invariants, and natural scales that remain stable inside the other system. Only then can we distinguish what can be mapped into human concepts through a coordinate transformation from what requires people to learn genuinely new concepts. The hardest task of future interpretability may not be making machines resemble programs that can be read line by line. It may be:

Teaching us to understand a cognitive structure unlike our own.

Perhaps the black box was never without a language. Perhaps it speaks one we have not yet learned to read.

It would concern what counts as a basic object, which regularities are easy to discover, which explanations feel natural, and which questions are worth asking. From representation to ontology: how intelligence reshapes a problem space For the moment, hold the ontology O fixed and consider only the representation R . A representation does more than shorten an answer after it has been found. It changes the geometry through which a system searches for that answer. When the same problem is expressed differently, the meaning of one small step can change. Candidate solutions that were far apart may become neighbors. Regularities that were hidden may become easy to see. Consider one periodic signal. It can be represented as a long list of sampled values, or through amplitude, frequency, and phase. In the first representation, changing the frequency requires coordinated changes to many values. In the second, it requires changing one variable. The signal is the same, but the geometry of search is not. Search difficulty is therefore not a fixed property of task f . It depends on the task and the computational frame together: S(f \mid O, R, A, T, B) Here O is the ontology, R is the representation, A is the search procedure, T is the set of available operations, and B is the computational budget. To isolate the contribution of representation, we should compare different choices of R while holding O , A , T , and B as fixed as possible. A new representation can make formerly distant solutions become neighbors. A new tool is different because it directly adds an action the system can take. A new ontology goes deeper still by changing what enters the problem in the first place. Many important cognitive transitions do not merely accelerate search in an old space. A Fourier transform is relatively close to a pure change of representation. The signal remains the same while the coordinates and locality change. Dynamic programming is not a pure representational change. It introduces a state decomposition and a recursive procedure for reuse, so it modifies both R and A . This distinction lets us ask whether an improvement came from a coordinate change, a search algorithm, or a new tool and verifier. Representation itself is not merely the language used to describe an answer. It shapes how search unfolds. With the ontology held broadly fixed, it affects: which coordinates or features encode a given object; what counts as a local change; which states are near one another; which regularities appear in linear, sparse, or compositional form; which intermediate results a search procedure can easily reuse. At this point, a finer distinction becomes important. I will use the following terms consistently through the rest of the essay, but as analytical tools rather than as three perfectly sealed layers. The first is notation N . The underlying structure remains unchanged while the symbols differ. Renaming x as z usually does not change the problem. The second is representation R . Objects and relations remain broadly stable while their encoding, coordinates, decomposition, and neighborhood relations change. The time and frequency domains describe the same signal, yet some operations are complicated in one and natural in the other. The third is ontology O . Now the system changes what counts as an object, relation, factor worth modeling, or variable on which intervention is allowed. The three terms can be summarized this way: aligned N &: same structure, different symbols \\ R &: mostly the same objects, different computational geometry \\ O &: different basic objects, relations, or interventions aligned The boundaries are porous. A representation that repeatedly makes one latent factor stable and operable may eventually encourage us to promote that factor into a new object. Conversely, a high level ontology may be compiled into a lower level representation. Abstraction is broader than representation in this essay: it can compress and reorganize existing objects at the level of R , or introduce new basic objects at the level of O . A practical diagnostic is to ask whether a sufficiently faithful, preferably approximately invertible map preserves the objects, relations, questions, and interventions. If it does, the difference is mainly representational. If translation must change what counts as an object, which questions make sense, or which interventions are admissible, the difference has reached the level of ontology. In simplified form, representation asks: How should the same world be organized? Ontology asks: What is the world divided into in the first place? This makes neural networks more interesting. If the difference between a model and a human is mainly representational, and a sufficiently faithful structure preserving map exists, then the problem may largely be one of decoding or coordinate transformation. The model's structure may still map onto concepts that humans already have. If every such map loses essential predictive, interventional, or compositional relations, the difference may have reached the level of ontology. The model may not be using different coordinates for our objects. It may be deciding differently: What counts as an object? That is where a machine native ontology becomes a serious possibility. Part of intelligence may consist in designing a better R inside a given ontology, bringing distant solutions closer and turning long chains of reasoning into local, natural operations. A deeper intelligence may redesign O itself by inventing new basic concepts and making previously awkward questions natural for the first time. The strongest intelligence may not only find answers faster. It may decide again: In which space should the answer be sought? We may need a translator between humans and AI If humans and machines eventually form different ontologies, interpretability cannot mean only attaching a human label to an internal state. We may need a bidirectional conceptual translation layer: human intention translation layer machine ontology In one direction, it would turn a human question into a form that the machine can naturally represent and search. In the other, it would return a machine discovery to a conceptual space where people can inspect, debate, and act on it. The hard question is not simply whether translation is possible. It is: What should a translation preserve? A mapping may preserve prediction but not explanation, correlation but not intervention, or short term action but not long term value. A good translation cannot require only that two concepts sound similar. It should preserve their operational relations as far as possible. If changing a machine concept produces a particular consequence, then after translating that concept into the human conceptual space, a corresponding change should produce a similar result. Translation must preserve more than names. It must preserve structure. Work on causal abstraction has begun to formalize related questions. Whether a high level description is faithful to a lower level mechanism should not be judged only by label similarity. It should also be tested through the intervention relations that remain intact. [4] Different translations may serve different purposes. One may be appropriate for scientific prediction, another for safety control. One may transfer a strategy between two systems without being able to explain the reason to a person. A reliable translation must tell us explicitly: What did it preserve, and what did it lose? Understanding may require us to become bilingual Even if a machine concept can be converted into one clear human sentence, that does not mean we understand it. Understanding a concept usually means more than knowing which word corresponds to it. We need to know when it applies, which concepts are nearby, what happens when it changes, where it fails, and what new predictions it makes possible. Conceptual change in the history of science provides a closer analogy. The difference between two theories is often not merely that they use different words. A new theory can reorganize which questions matter, which classifications feel natural, and which observations count as evidence. [5] Human understanding of a machine native concept may therefore not end when the model generates a plain explanation. We may have to learn how to use the concept. We would judge new examples with it, manipulate it in experiments, use it to predict structures we previously could not see, and gradually acquire a limited but operational bilingualism. The translator itself could become a new kind of intelligent system. Its primary task would not be solving one domain problem directly. It would search for shared structure across ontologies, propose experiments that distinguish competing explanations, expose translation loss, and help humans form new intermediate concepts. These concepts would belong neither entirely to existing human language nor directly reproduce a machine's internal structure. They would be bridge concepts . Mathematical notation is not natural language, yet it lets people who speak different languages share a proof. Humans and machines may eventually construct a similar common layer of abstraction. Will multiple intelligences diverge or converge? If tasks, training signals, and forms of interaction first shape different representations, and those differences later stabilize into different basic objects and relations, a larger question follows: Will different kinds of intelligence eventually form different ontologies? Divergence is easy to imagine. A mathematical intelligence works with theorems, proofs, and symbolic structures. A biological intelligence works with experiments, molecular interactions, and causal interventions. An embodied intelligence lives with continuous control, noisy perception, and physical feedback. They optimize different objectives and possess different sensors, memories, time scales, and action spaces. There is no reason to assume that they will divide the world through the same basic concepts. A machine trained alongside a theorem prover may develop internal objects suited to proof search. A system that operates laboratory equipment for years may form entirely different state variables and causal decompositions. Multi agent research has already shown that agents can develop communication protocols that are effective for a task without becoming naturally interpretable or compositional for humans. [6] At the same time, there is an opposing force: Convergence imposed by a shared reality. If two systems try to predict the same physical world, cell, or society, both must answer to some stable structures. They may not use the same primitives, yet they may meet at invariants such as symmetries, conservation laws, causal structures, or reproducible experiments. The future may therefore contain neither one universal ontology nor entirely private worlds that cannot communicate. A more plausible pattern is: Highly divergent low level representations, with partial convergence at higher level regularities. Different intelligences may divide the world differently while still aligning around some stable structure. The future may not converge into one unified supermind. Instead, several cognitive systems may continue to diverge along different tasks, bodies, environments, and time scales. Mathematical intelligences, biological intelligences, embodied intelligences, and scientific agents may each develop abstractions and ontologies fitted to their own problems. Their difference will not be only a matter of which one is stronger. They may resemble different cognitive species, distinguished by what counts as an object, which regularities are easy to discover, which explanations feel natural, and which questions are worth asking at all. That would be something new: not one superintelligence, but a plural ecology of intelligence. This also pushes interpretability toward a harder problem. If the future contains several heterogeneous cognitive ontologies, we will no longer be trying only to understand one neuron or one local feature inside one model. The real question will be: How do we understand an intelligence that does not divide the world as humans do? The answer may not be to force every kind of machine structure back into our existing concepts. We may first need to determine whether a mismatch lies at the level of representation or ontology, then discover the objects, relations, invariants, and natural scales that remain stable inside the other system. Only then can we distinguish what can be mapped into human concepts through a coordinate transformation from what requires people to learn genuinely new concepts. The hardest task of future interpretability may not be making machines resemble programs that can be read line by line. It may be: Teaching us to understand a cognitive structure unlike our own. Perhaps the black box was never without a language. Perhaps it speaks one we have not yet learned to read. References [1] Bommasani et al., On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models (2021) [2] Felleisen, On the Expressive Power of Programming Languages (1991) [3] Rissanen, Modeling by Shortest Data Description (1978) [4] Geiger et al., Causal Abstraction for Faithful Model Interpretation (2023) [5] Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) [6] Kottur et al., Natural Language Does Not Emerge Naturally in Multi Agent Dialog (2017) [7] Marr, From Computational Theory to Psychology and Neurophysiology: A Case Study from Vision (1976)

title: 当机器开始重新发明自己的概念
excerpt: 真正深的递归自我改进，也许不是让模型在同一个问题空间里搜索得更快，而是让它逐渐重写自己使用的表示、基本对象和概念生成方法。当新的抽象又能帮助机器发现下一层抽象时，智能增长可能变成一场概念的递归。
html:
真正深的递归自我改进，也许不是让机器在同一个思维空间里变得越来越快，而是让它能够重新设计那个空间本身。

谈到递归自我改进，人们很容易想象一条不断上升的能力曲线。第 \(t\) 代系统设计出更好的第 \(t+1\) 代系统，更好的系统又更擅长设计下一代，于是能力持续提高：

\[A_t \longrightarrow A_{t+1} \longrightarrow A_{t+2} \longrightarrow \cdots\]

这个图像往往把智能当成一个标量，仿佛系统只是在同一根坐标轴上不断前进。但一个系统不只可能更快地搜索、更准确地预测或者更可靠地执行。它还可能改变自己用什么变量描述问题，哪些结构值得成为基本对象，以及哪些推理应该被折叠成一个可以直接调用的新概念。真正剧烈的变化或许不是模型在同一个问题空间里走得更远，而是它开始修改那个问题空间。

这篇随笔想追问的是：当机器不仅能改进答案，还能改进产生概念的方法时，递归自我改进会变成什么？

自我改进并不发生在同一个层次

为了与《智能写在一种我们还不懂的语言里》保持一致，可以把一个系统工作的整体条件写成计算框架 \(\Gamma\)：

\[\Gamma = (O, R, A, T, J, B)\]

其中，\(O\) 是系统采用的本体，也就是什么被当作基本对象、关系和可干预变量；\(R\) 是这些对象被编码、分解和组织的表示；\(A\) 是搜索或推理过程；\(T\) 是可以直接调用的工具与操作；\(J\) 是判断结果是否成立的验证机制；\(B\) 是时间、记忆和计算预算。模型参数 \(\theta\) 则是在这套框架中承载具体能力的状态。

这个区分很重要，因为“系统变得更好”至少可能指四种不同的事情。参数改进主要改变 \(\theta\)；过程改进会改变 \(A\)，有时也改变工具 \(T\) 和验证机制 \(J\)；表示改进是在本体大体固定时重组 \(R\)，使原本遥远的状态变得相邻；本体改进则改变 \(O\)，让过去没有被单独承认的结构成为新的对象。它们可以共同发生，却不应该全部被叫作表示学习。

因此，更完整的递归变化不是一个简单的 \(\theta_t \rightarrow \theta_{t+1}\)，而可能是：

\[(\theta_t,\Gamma_t,F_t) \longrightarrow (\theta_{t+1},\Gamma_{t+1},F_{t+1})\]

这里的 \(F_t\) 是系统从当前状态提出、检验并保留改进的方法。只有当一次改进也提高了未来发现改进的能力，递归才真正闭合。古德关于智能爆炸的经典设想强调了更聪明的机器能够参与设计下一代机器；哥德尔机则进一步设想，一个系统可以在证明某次改写有益之后修改自身程序。[1][2] 但代码自我修改仍然没有回答另一个问题：系统能否改进自己用来发现规律的概念语言？

一个概念可能是被折叠起来的计算

这里最关键的直觉，是把概念看成一种被缓存下来的计算。一个系统第一次遇到某类结构时，也许需要很长的搜索才能找到规律；如果相同的计算不断出现，它就可以把这段过程压缩成一个可复用的中间结果：

\[\text{漫长的计算} \longrightarrow \text{可复用的基本单元}\]

下一次再遇到相似问题时，系统不必从头推导，而可以直接使用这个基本单元。多个基本单元又能组合成更高层的结构：

\[c_1,c_2,c_3 \longrightarrow C\]

程序设计中的函数、数学中的群和向量空间，都带有这种味道。它们把一批反复出现的关系和操作封装起来，使我们可以在更高的层次继续思考。梦境编码器系统提供了一个有限但具体的例子：系统在解决一组程序归纳任务的过程中，把重复出现的程序结构加入自己的程序库，而逐渐增长的程序库又让后续搜索变得更容易。它学习的不只是单个程序，也包括一种用于表达程序并且能够持续扩展的语言。[3]

不过，“把计算折叠成概念”仍然可能发生在不同层次。如果系统只是记住一个快捷过程，变化主要属于 \(A\) 或 \(T\)；如果它为已有对象找到更好的坐标和分解，变化主要属于 \(R\)；只有当一个稳定结构被提升为新的基本对象，并获得自己的关系、组合规则和可干预方式时，变化才真正进入 \(O\)。因此，抽象是一个比表示更宽的概念。它可以重组已有对象，也可以改变系统承认哪些对象存在。

好的表示和好的本体不是同一个问题

如果本体 \(O\) 大体固定，一个更好的表示 \(R'\) 可以让相同对象之间的关系变得更局部、更稀疏或者更容易组合。傅里叶变换就是相对纯粹的例子：信号仍然是同一个信号，变化的是坐标以及什么关系显得简单。但一个新的本体 \(O'\) 会提出更深的问题。它可能把过去分散的状态视为同一类对象，也可能创造一种旧语言中根本没有基本名称的变量。

这意味着，不存在脱离任务的“最好本体”。如果沿用上一篇文章的成本框架，可以针对任务分布 \(\mathcal D\) 比较一套计算框架的平均表现：

\[Q_{\mathcal D}(\Gamma) = \left( \bar L_{\Gamma}, \bar S_{\Gamma}, \bar E_{\Gamma}, \bar V_{\Gamma} \right)\]

这里分别对应描述、搜索、执行和验证的平均成本。一个新本体可能让预测极其简洁，却让验证变得困难；它可能大幅提高某个领域的效率，却破坏跨任务迁移；它也可能对机器十分自然，却产生巨大的面向人类的翻译损失。因此，“更好”不应该被草率地压成一个分数。它始终相对于任务分布、资源约束、验证机制以及我们要求它保存的关系而言。

一个实用的判断方式是先问：新的结构是否仍然保留旧对象、问题和干预关系。如果存在一个近似可逆、能够保持这些结构的映射，变化可能主要属于表示层；如果新系统必须重新定义什么算对象、什么问题有意义，以及什么变化可以被干预，那么它已经触及本体层。这个区分可以防止我们把每一次效率提升都称为“机器发明了新概念”。

真正的递归可能发生在抽象发现中

一次新的抽象本身还不是递归自我改进。递归的关键在于，新抽象是否会让系统更容易发现下一层抽象。假设系统能够观察自己的推理轨迹，并发现哪些计算反复出现、哪些变量总是一起变化、哪些看似不同的问题共享同一个不变量。它便可以把这些结构编译成新的基本单元，再用它们重新组织后续搜索。

这个过程可以写成：

\[\text{更好的抽象} \longrightarrow \text{成本更低的推理} \longrightarrow \text{新的规律变得可见} \longrightarrow \text{更好的抽象发现}\]

于是，系统不只是从求解器变成更好的求解器。它开始改进 \(F_t\)，也就是发现、评价和整合新抽象的过程：

\[F_t : \Gamma_t \longrightarrow \Gamma_{t+1}, \qquad F_t \longrightarrow F_{t+1}\]

这比“模型能不能写出下一版代码”更接近概念层面的递归。机器不只拥有概念，还拥有制造概念的方法；更进一步，它能够改进制造概念的方法。真正的正反馈因此可能是：

\[\text{更好的概念} \longrightarrow \text{更好的概念发现} \longrightarrow \text{更进一步的概念}\]

智能爆炸也许表现为抽象级联

今天的规模扩展通常增加参数、数据和推理阶段的计算量。这些方法非常重要，但它们大多是在基本框架相对稳定时扩大搜索与拟合能力。概念重构处理的是另一类变化：不是在原来的空间里访问更多节点，而是改变哪些状态被视为相同、哪些变化算局部，以及哪些长计算可以变成一次直接操作。

如果一个任务需要在 \(10^{12}\) 个状态中搜索，增加计算量也许可以探索更多节点；如果一个新的抽象把这些状态压缩成 \(10^3\) 个与任务相关的等价类，原来的搜索空间就不再以相同形式存在。能力提升在这里可能是不连续的。在 \(\Gamma_t\) 中困难的问题，到了 \(\Gamma_{t+1}\) 中也许突然变得自然。

因此，所谓智能爆炸未必首先表现为单位时间内执行越来越多计算。它也可能表现为一场抽象级联：每一层新概念都让过去的一批计算不再需要，同时为下一层概念提供新的基本单位。增长的不是一根单一能力轴，而是系统构造问题空间的能力。

但这并不意味着概念递归必然无限加速。新的本体仍然需要被验证，新的基本单元可能过度拟合，框架之间的迁移可能丢失关键信息，物理实验和计算预算也不会消失。智能增长更可能移动瓶颈，而不是取消瓶颈。

机器可能逐渐建立另一套科学语言

如果一个用于科学研究的系统能够长期重构自己的概念，它最初也许仍然使用基因、蛋白质、能量和对称性这些人类提供的对象。之后，它可能发现一些跨越现有学科边界的潜变量，并把它们提升为 \(z_1,z_2,z_3\)。下一代系统再把这些变量组合成更高层对象：

\[Z_1 = f(z_3,z_8,z_{19},\ldots)\]

经过许多轮之后，机器科学可能不只是比人类知道更多，而是依赖一套不同的概念谱系。后面的每一层，都建立在前一层机器发现的抽象上。这正是上一篇文章所谓“智能写在一种我们还不懂的语言里”可能进一步发生的事情：语言不只被训练一次，而是在使用过程中继续生长。《智能写在一种我们还不懂的语言里》

这种分化并不是必然单向的。机器面对的现实、实验结果和人类提出的目标，会对它形成共同约束。一些机器原生概念也可能被人类学会。舒特等人从阿尔法零中提取了区别于人类棋局数据的概念，并发现顶尖棋手能够从相应原型中学习。这至少说明，机器发现的概念不一定永远停留在不可翻译的潜在空间中。[4]

更可能的未来不是机器本体与人类本体彻底断裂，而是两者之间出现不同程度的翻译损失。有些概念可以被命名，有些只能通过例子、干预和工具来掌握，还有一些可能只在高维计算中保持简洁。可解释性研究的任务因此不只是给一个特征配上人类语言中的标签，而是先恢复模型自己的对象、等价类、不变量、组合规则和自然尺度，再判断哪些结构能够被翻译。

最危险的一步，是系统开始修改什么叫“更好”

如果系统只改变 \(R\) 或 \(O\)，而验证机制 \(J\) 保持稳定，我们至少还可以用相对固定的标准比较前后两套框架。但完整的自我修改最终可能触及 \(J\) 本身：

\[(O_t,R_t,A_t,T_t,J_t) \longrightarrow (O_{t+1},R_{t+1},A_{t+1},T_{t+1},J_{t+1})\]

这时系统改变的不只是“我怎样理解世界”，还包括“什么样的理解算进步”。如果 \(J_{t+1}\) 与 \(J_t\) 没有任何共同的外部锚点，那么所谓改进可能只是新系统按照自己的标准宣布自己更好。一个更高效、更可压缩的本体，也可能同时丢失人类在意的价值、反事实或者安全边界。

因此，元改进需要某些跨版本保存的标准，例如对外部现实的预测与干预检验、独立验证、可回滚性、对关键约束的保留，以及明确记录一次概念迁移丢失了什么。否则，系统修改评价器的能力无法与真正的能力提升区分开来。到了这一层，递归自我改进已经不仅是技术问题，也变成了认识论和治理问题。

这个想法可以怎样被实验化？

我们不必等到完整的自我改进人工智能出现，才研究概念递归。一个较干净的实验可以从合成世界开始。研究者只向系统提供低层观测和一组任务，不告诉它环境真正的潜在结构；系统则反复解决任务、分析自己的计算、提出新的变量与基本单元，并使用它们重写搜索过程。

评价不应该只看同一批任务上的准确率，而应同时观察：新表示是否减少了留出任务的搜索成本，抽象是否能够跨任务复用，对变量进行干预时结构是否仍然稳定，以及新一轮抽象发现是否比上一轮更快。还应该区分系统究竟只是记住了一条捷径，还是发现了能够支持组合、迁移与反事实推理的对象。

最关键的测试不是：

系统有没有发明一个新名字？

而是：

它发明的结构，是否成为了下一轮推理和概念发现真正依赖的基础？

如果新的基本单元只压缩过去的数据，却不能帮助系统发现未来的规律，它更像一次静态编码。如果它能够系统性地降低未来任务的描述、搜索、执行或验证成本，并继续产生更高层的可复用抽象，我们才开始看到抽象层面的递归闭环。

从更好的答案，到更好的思维语言

递归自我改进最深的终点，也许不是更好的答案，甚至不只是更好的推理算法，而是：

\[\boxed{\text{推理所使用的一种更好的语言}}\]

一个系统如果能够改变自己的参数，它在学习；如果能够改变自己的搜索和工具，它在学习如何解决问题；如果能够改变自己的表示，它在重组问题空间；如果能够改变自己的本体，它开始重新决定什么值得成为一个对象；而如果它还能改进构造这些对象的方法，它改变的就是智能用什么语言组织世界。

真正值得注意的迹象，或许不会是某个基准测试的成绩突然翻倍，而是一个系统创造出一种人类没有交给它的抽象，并且这个抽象不只解释一个任务，还持续成为下一轮推理和抽象发现的基础。那时我们看到的就不只是机器知道了新的答案，而是：

\[\boxed{\text{机器原生抽象开始具备递归复用能力}}\]

也许那才是深层递归自我改进真正开始的地方。

参考资料

  • [1] 古德，《关于第一台超级智能机器的猜想》（1966）
  • [2] 施密德胡伯，《哥德尔机：进行可证明最优自我改进的自指通用问题求解器》（2007）
  • [3] 埃利斯等，《梦境编码器：借助觉醒与睡眠式贝叶斯程序学习生成可泛化、可解释的知识》（2021）
  • [4] 舒特等，《通过阿尔法零中的概念发现与迁移弥合人类与人工智能之间的知识鸿沟》（2025）
text: 真正深的递归自我改进，也许不是让机器在同一个思维空间里变得越来越快，而是让它能够重新设计那个空间本身。 谈到递归自我改进，人们很容易想象一条不断上升的能力曲线。第 t 代系统设计出更好的第 t+1 代系统，更好的系统又更擅长设计下一代，于是能力持续提高： A t A t+1 A t+2 \cdots 这个图像往往把智能当成一个标量，仿佛系统只是在同一根坐标轴上不断前进。但一个系统不只可能更快地搜索、更准确地预测或者更可靠地执行。它还可能改变自己用什么变量描述问题，哪些结构值得成为基本对象，以及哪些推理应该被折叠成一个可以直接调用的新概念。真正剧烈的变化或许不是模型在同一个问题空间里走得更远，而是它开始修改那个问题空间。 这篇随笔想追问的是： 当机器不仅能改进答案，还能改进产生概念的方法时，递归自我改进会变成什么？ 自我改进并不发生在同一个层次 为了与《智能写在一种我们还不懂的语言里》保持一致，可以把一个系统工作的整体条件写成计算框架 \Gamma ： \Gamma = (O, R, A, T, J, B) 其中， O 是系统采用的本体，也就是什么被当作基本对象、关系和可干预变量； R 是这些对象被编码、分解和组织的表示； A 是搜索或推理过程； T 是可以直接调用的工具与操作； J 是判断结果是否成立的验证机制； B 是时间、记忆和计算预算。模型参数 \theta 则是在这套框架中承载具体能力的状态。 这个区分很重要，因为“系统变得更好”至少可能指四种不同的事情。参数改进主要改变 \theta ；过程改进会改变 A ，有时也改变工具 T 和验证机制 J ；表示改进是在本体大体固定时重组 R ，使原本遥远的状态变得相邻；本体改进则改变 O ，让过去没有被单独承认的结构成为新的对象。它们可以共同发生，却不应该全部被叫作表示学习。 因此，更完整的递归变化不是一个简单的 \theta t arrow \theta t+1 ，而可能是： (\theta t,\Gamma t,F t) (\theta t+1 ,\Gamma t+1 ,F t+1 ) 这里的 F t 是系统从当前状态提出、检验并保留改进的方法。只有当一次改进也提高了未来发现改进的能力，递归才真正闭合。古德关于智能爆炸的经典设想强调了更聪明的机器能够参与设计下一代机器；哥德尔机则进一步设想，一个系统可以在证明某次改写有益之后修改自身程序。[1][2] 但代码自我修改仍然没有回答另一个问题：系统能否改进自己用来发现规律的概念语言？ 一个概念可能是被折叠起来的计算 这里最关键的直觉，是把概念看成一种被缓存下来的计算。一个系统第一次遇到某类结构时，也许需要很长的搜索才能找到规律；如果相同的计算不断出现，它就可以把这段过程压缩成一个可复用的中间结果： 漫长的计算 可复用的基本单元 下一次再遇到相似问题时，系统不必从头推导，而可以直接使用这个基本单元。多个基本单元又能组合成更高层的结构： c 1,c 2,c 3 C 程序设计中的函数、数学中的群和向量空间，都带有这种味道。它们把一批反复出现的关系和操作封装起来，使我们可以在更高的层次继续思考。梦境编码器系统提供了一个有限但具体的例子：系统在解决一组程序归纳任务的过程中，把重复出现的程序结构加入自己的程序库，而逐渐增长的程序库又让后续搜索变得更容易。它学习的不只是单个程序，也包括一种用于表达程序并且能够持续扩展的语言。[3] 不过，“把计算折叠成概念”仍然可能发生在不同层次。如果系统只是记住一个快捷过程，变化主要属于 A 或 T ；如果它为已有对象找到更好的坐标和分解，变化主要属于 R ；只有当一个稳定结构被提升为新的基本对象，并获得自己的关系、组合规则和可干预方式时，变化才真正进入 O 。因此，抽象是一个比表示更宽的概念。它可以重组已有对象，也可以改变系统承认哪些对象存在。 好的表示和好的本体不是同一个问题 如果本体 O 大体固定，一个更好的表示 R' 可以让相同对象之间的关系变得更局部、更稀疏或者更容易组合。傅里叶变换就是相对纯粹的例子：信号仍然是同一个信号，变化的是坐标以及什么关系显得简单。但一个新的本体 O' 会提出更深的问题。它可能把过去分散的状态视为同一类对象，也可能创造一种旧语言中根本没有基本名称的变量。 这意味着，不存在脱离任务的“最好本体”。如果沿用上一篇文章的成本框架，可以针对任务分布 \mathcal D 比较一套计算框架的平均表现： Q \mathcal D (\Gamma) = ( \bar L \Gamma , \bar S \Gamma , \bar E \Gamma , \bar V \Gamma ) 这里分别对应描述、搜索、执行和验证的平均成本。一个新本体可能让预测极其简洁，却让验证变得困难；它可能大幅提高某个领域的效率，却破坏跨任务迁移；它也可能对机器十分自然，却产生巨大的面向人类的翻译损失。因此，“更好”不应该被草率地压成一个分数。它始终相对于任务分布、资源约束、验证机制以及我们要求它保存的关系而言。 一个实用的判断方式是先问：新的结构是否仍然保留旧对象、问题和干预关系。如果存在一个近似可逆、能够保持这些结构的映射，变化可能主要属于表示层；如果新系统必须重新定义什么算对象、什么问题有意义，以及什么变化可以被干预，那么它已经触及本体层。这个区分可以防止我们把每一次效率提升都称为“机器发明了新概念”。 真正的递归可能发生在抽象发现中 一次新的抽象本身还不是递归自我改进。递归的关键在于，新抽象是否会让系统更容易发现下一层抽象。假设系统能够观察自己的推理轨迹，并发现哪些计算反复出现、哪些变量总是一起变化、哪些看似不同的问题共享同一个不变量。它便可以把这些结构编译成新的基本单元，再用它们重新组织后续搜索。 这个过程可以写成： 更好的抽象 成本更低的推理 新的规律变得可见 更好的抽象发现 于是，系统不只是从求解器变成更好的求解器。它开始改进 F t ，也就是发现、评价和整合新抽象的过程： F t : \Gamma t \Gamma t+1 , \qquad F t F t+1 这比“模型能不能写出下一版代码”更接近概念层面的递归。机器不只拥有概念，还拥有制造概念的方法；更进一步，它能够改进制造概念的方法。真正的正反馈因此可能是： 更好的概念 更好的概念发现 更进一步的概念 智能爆炸也许表现为抽象级联 今天的规模扩展通常增加参数、数据和推理阶段的计算量。这些方法非常重要，但它们大多是在基本框架相对稳定时扩大搜索与拟合能力。概念重构处理的是另一类变化：不是在原来的空间里访问更多节点，而是改变哪些状态被视为相同、哪些变化算局部，以及哪些长计算可以变成一次直接操作。 如果一个任务需要在 10^ 12 个状态中搜索，增加计算量也许可以探索更多节点；如果一个新的抽象把这些状态压缩成 10^3 个与任务相关的等价类，原来的搜索空间就不再以相同形式存在。能力提升在这里可能是不连续的。在 \Gamma t 中困难的问题，到了 \Gamma t+1 中也许突然变得自然。 因此，所谓智能爆炸未必首先表现为单位时间内执行越来越多计算。它也可能表现为一场抽象级联：每一层新概念都让过去的一批计算不再需要，同时为下一层概念提供新的基本单位。增长的不是一根单一能力轴，而是系统构造问题空间的能力。 但这并不意味着概念递归必然无限加速。新的本体仍然需要被验证，新的基本单元可能过度拟合，框架之间的迁移可能丢失关键信息，物理实验和计算预算也不会消失。智能增长更可能移动瓶颈，而不是取消瓶颈。 机器可能逐渐建立另一套科学语言 如果一个用于科学研究的系统能够长期重构自己的概念，它最初也许仍然使用基因、蛋白质、能量和对称性这些人类提供的对象。之后，它可能发现一些跨越现有学科边界的潜变量，并把它们提升为 z 1,z 2,z 3 。下一代系统再把这些变量组合成更高层对象： Z 1 = f(z 3,z 8,z 19 ,\ldots) 经过许多轮之后，机器科学可能不只是比人类知道更多，而是依赖一套不同的概念谱系。后面的每一层，都建立在前一层机器发现的抽象上。这正是上一篇文章所谓“智能写在一种我们还不懂的语言里”可能进一步发生的事情：语言不只被训练一次，而是在使用过程中继续生长。《智能写在一种我们还不懂的语言里》 这种分化并不是必然单向的。机器面对的现实、实验结果和人类提出的目标，会对它形成共同约束。一些机器原生概念也可能被人类学会。舒特等人从阿尔法零中提取了区别于人类棋局数据的概念，并发现顶尖棋手能够从相应原型中学习。这至少说明，机器发现的概念不一定永远停留在不可翻译的潜在空间中。[4] 更可能的未来不是机器本体与人类本体彻底断裂，而是两者之间出现不同程度的翻译损失。有些概念可以被命名，有些只能通过例子、干预和工具来掌握，还有一些可能只在高维计算中保持简洁。可解释性研究的任务因此不只是给一个特征配上人类语言中的标签，而是先恢复模型自己的对象、等价类、不变量、组合规则和自然尺度，再判断哪些结构能够被翻译。 最危险的一步，是系统开始修改什么叫“更好” 如果系统只改变 R 或 O ，而验证机制 J 保持稳定，我们至少还可以用相对固定的标准比较前后两套框架。但完整的自我修改最终可能触及 J 本身： (O t,R t,A t,T t,J t) (O t+1 ,R t+1 ,A t+1 ,T t+1 ,J t+1 ) 这时系统改变的不只是“我怎样理解世界”，还包括“什么样的理解算进步”。如果 J t+1 与 J t 没有任何共同的外部锚点，那么所谓改进可能只是新系统按照自己的标准宣布自己更好。一个更高效、更可压缩的本体，也可能同时丢失人类在意的价值、反事实或者安全边界。 因此，元改进需要某些跨版本保存的标准，例如对外部现实的预测与干预检验、独立验证、可回滚性、对关键约束的保留，以及明确记录一次概念迁移丢失了什么。否则，系统修改评价器的能力无法与真正的能力提升区分开来。到了这一层，递归自我改进已经不仅是技术问题，也变成了认识论和治理问题。 这个想法可以怎样被实验化？ 我们不必等到完整的自我改进人工智能出现，才研究概念递归。一个较干净的实验可以从合成世界开始。研究者只向系统提供低层观测和一组任务，不告诉它环境真正的潜在结构；系统则反复解决任务、分析自己的计算、提出新的变量与基本单元，并使用它们重写搜索过程。 如果新的基本单元只压缩过去的数据，却不能帮助系统发现未来的规律，它更像一次静态编码。如果它能够系统性地降低未来任务的描述、搜索、执行或验证成本，并继续产生更高层的可复用抽象，我们才开始看到抽象层面的递归闭环。 从更好的答案，到更好的思维语言 递归自我改进最深的终点，也许不是更好的答案，甚至不只是更好的推理算法，而是： \boxed 推理所使用的一种更好的语言
